subject: physics

items.q: Which statement correctly classifies nuclear fuel and gives the correct reason?
items.correct: Non-renewable, because the uranium used is not replenished as it is used
items.misconception: Renewable, because generating with it does not release any carbon dioxide
items.why: Students merge two separate ideas - 'renewable' and 'low-carbon' - into a single category of 'good' resources, because the two usually go together for wind, solar and tidal. Keep the two questions apart. Is it replenished as it is used? That decides renewable or non-renewable. Does it release carbon dioxide? That is a separate environmental question. Nuclear fuel answers no to both.
items.random_wrong: Non-renewable, because nuclear fuel is one of the fossil fuels found in rock

items.q: Which group contains only renewable energy resources?
items.correct: Bio-fuel, geothermal and water waves
items.misconception: Nuclear fuel, geothermal and the tides
items.why: Students merge two separate ideas - 'renewable' and 'low-carbon' - into a single category of 'good' resources, because the two usually go together for wind, solar and tidal. Keep the two questions apart. Is it replenished as it is used? That decides renewable or non-renewable. Does it release carbon dioxide? That is a separate environmental question. Nuclear fuel answers no to both.
items.random_wrong: Bio-fuel, water waves and natural gas

items.q: Which of these is the correct definition of a renewable energy resource?
items.correct: One that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used
items.misconception: One that will never run out, however quickly it is used up
items.why: The everyday sense of 'renewable' suggests endlessness, and students meet the word alongside phrases like 'the wind will always blow'. The definition is about replacement keeping pace with use, not about an infinite store. Focus on the specification's wording: the resource is being replenished as it is used. Bio-fuel is renewable only because crops are grown again; if they were not replanted it would run out. The test is replacement, not size of supply.
items.random_wrong: One that gives out no carbon dioxide at all when it is used

items.q: Why is bio-fuel classified as a renewable energy resource?
items.correct: Because the plants used to make it are grown again as it is used
items.misconception: Because burning bio-fuel causes no environmental damage at all
items.why: The 'bio' prefix and the idea of a growing crop signal natural and safe, and the fact that the fuel is still burned is easily overlooked. Bio-fuel is burned like any other fuel, so carbon dioxide is released. Add the land-use impact: crops grown for fuel occupy ground that could feed people, and natural habitat is sometimes cleared to grow them.
items.random_wrong: Because burning bio-fuel releases no carbon dioxide into the air

items.q: New coal is still forming underground today. Why is coal still classed as non-renewable?
items.correct: It forms far more slowly than it is used, so it is not replenished
items.misconception: Non-renewable resources are the ones that give off polluting gases
items.why: Students merge two separate ideas - 'renewable' and 'low-carbon' - into a single category of 'good' resources, because the two usually go together for wind, solar and tidal. Keep the two questions apart. Is it replenished as it is used? That decides renewable or non-renewable. Does it release carbon dioxide? That is a separate environmental question. Nuclear fuel answers no to both.
items.random_wrong: Non-renewable resources are the ones that supply energy reliably

items.q: Which one of these energy resources is non-renewable?
items.correct: Nuclear fuel, from uranium that is mined from rock
items.misconception: Hydro-electricity, using water held behind a dam
items.why: The specification lists both, and both are named after water, so students collapse them into one category and then cannot list nine separate resources. Sort by where the energy comes from: hydro-electricity from water stored high up behind a dam, water waves from the moving surface of the sea, the tides from the daily rise and fall of sea level. Three different entries in the list.
items.random_wrong: Bio-fuel, made from crops that are grown for burning

items.q: Which energy resource supplies most of the energy used for transport worldwide?
items.correct: Oil, which is refined into petrol, diesel and aviation fuel
items.misconception: Coal, which is burned in the engines of most road vehicles
items.why: Energy resources are usually first met in the context of power stations, so 'fossil fuel' becomes tied to that single use in students' minds. Track oil in particular: petrol and diesel for road transport, aviation fuel for aircraft, oil and gas burned in boilers for heating, as well as gas burned in power stations. One resource, three uses.
items.random_wrong: Electricity, because all vehicles now run on rechargeable batteries

items.q: A house is heated by burning natural gas in a boiler. Which statement about this is correct?
items.correct: Gas is a non-renewable fossil fuel, used here for heating
items.misconception: Gas is only ever used to generate electricity, never for heating
items.why: Students meet electric heaters and kettles, and do not connect the gas boiler or wood burner with the same list of energy resources. Most heating of buildings burns gas, oil or wood directly - no electricity involved. Geothermal energy and solar water heating also heat directly. Heating is its own use, and different resources suit it.
items.random_wrong: Gas is renewable, because new gas keeps forming under the sea

items.q: Which resource can be used for all three of transport, electricity generation and heating?
items.correct: Bio-fuel, which is burned in vehicles, power stations and boilers
items.misconception: Water waves, which can drive vehicles as well as power stations
items.why: Comparing resources by a single measure - renewable or not, clean or not - hides the fact that they are used in different ways and in different places. Compare use by use. Bio-fuel serves transport, generation and heating. Water waves and the tides realistically serve generation only. Oil dominates transport. Geothermal heats and generates, but only where the hot rock is.
items.random_wrong: Geothermal, which is used in vehicles and in power stations

items.q: Solar panels on a roof warm water for a house. Which use of energy resources is this?
items.correct: Heating, because energy from the Sun warms the water directly
items.misconception: Electricity generation, since solar panels always make electricity
items.why: Solar electricity is the version students see in the news, and both kinds of panel look similar from the ground. Distinguish the two uses. Solar water heating warms water for the building directly - no electricity is generated at any point. Sort solar examples by the use they serve, not by the fact that they are on a roof.
items.random_wrong: Electricity generation, since the hot water later drives a turbine

items.q: Why is a wind farm a less reliable energy resource than a gas-fired power station?
items.correct: The wind does not always blow, so output cannot be guaranteed
items.misconception: Wind turbines break down far more often than a gas power station
items.why: In everyday language an unreliable machine is a faulty one, and students carry that meaning across without noticing that the term describes the resource, not the hardware. The word describes availability of the resource. A wind turbine in perfect working order produces nothing on a still day. That is the sense in which wind is unreliable.
items.random_wrong: Each turbine transfers much less energy than a gas power station

items.q: Tidal energy is described as a reliable resource. Which statement explains why?
items.correct: The tides rise and fall in a regular, predictable daily cycle
items.misconception: The tides transfer far more energy than any other resource
items.why: 'Reliable', 'powerful' and 'good' merge into one vague idea of quality, and students have no separate slot for availability on demand. Test with a question: can it deliver at three in the morning in December? Geothermal and gas can, so they are reliable. Solar cannot, whatever the size of the array, so it is not.
items.random_wrong: Tidal equipment is stronger, so it hardly ever breaks down

items.q: A country needs electricity at all hours, in any weather. Which resources suit that best?
items.correct: Nuclear fuel and gas, because their output can be controlled
items.misconception: Wind and water waves, because there is always some wind
items.why: Students reason from the whole planet rather than from the site of the wind farm, and from 'the resource still exists' rather than 'the energy is available here, now, in the amount needed'. Reliability means energy is available when it is wanted. A still, cold, windless evening is exactly when demand is high and a wind farm delivers least. That is why wind is classed as unreliable.
items.random_wrong: Solar only, because sunlight reaches the ground each day

items.q: Which environmental impact arises mainly from burning fossil fuels?
items.correct: Carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere as the fuel burns
items.misconception: Radioactive waste that has to be stored safely for many years
items.why: Cooling towers releasing water vapour look exactly like the pictures used to illustrate pollution, and 'nuclear' already carries a strong sense of danger, so the two are merged. Match each resource to its own impact. Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide and, for coal and oil, sulfur dioxide. Nuclear fuel releases neither, but leaves radioactive waste needing secure storage for a very long time.
items.random_wrong: Loss of habitat when a river valley is flooded behind a dam

items.q: Which of these is an environmental impact of burning coal in a power station?
items.correct: Release of sulfur dioxide, which contributes to acid rain
items.misconception: Release of radioactive waste that must be stored for years
items.why: Cooling towers releasing water vapour look exactly like the pictures used to illustrate pollution, and 'nuclear' already carries a strong sense of danger, so the two are merged. Match each resource to its own impact. Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide and, for coal and oil, sulfur dioxide. Nuclear fuel releases neither, but leaves radioactive waste needing secure storage for a very long time.
items.random_wrong: Release of carbon dioxide, which then falls as acid rain

items.q: Which statement about the environmental impact of renewable resources is correct?
items.correct: Hydro-electric schemes can flood valleys and destroy habitats
items.misconception: Renewable resources have no environmental impact of any kind
items.why: Renewables are presented as the answer to the problems caused by fossil fuels, and the contrast is often drawn so sharply that students hear 'no impact' rather than 'less of one particular impact'. Name a specific impact for each renewable: hydro-electric dams flood valleys and destroy habitats, tidal schemes alter estuaries, wind farms bring noise and visual intrusion, bio-fuel crops take land that could grow food and release carbon dioxide when burned.
items.random_wrong: Growing crops for bio-fuel has no effect on land or wildlife

items.q: Which environmental impact is associated with the use of nuclear fuel?
items.correct: Radioactive waste that stays dangerous for a very long time
items.misconception: Large amounts of carbon dioxide released while generating
items.why: Cooling towers releasing water vapour look exactly like the pictures used to illustrate pollution, and 'nuclear' already carries a strong sense of danger, so the two are merged. Match each resource to its own impact. Fossil fuels release carbon dioxide and, for coal and oil, sulfur dioxide. Nuclear fuel releases neither, but leaves radioactive waste needing secure storage for a very long time.
items.random_wrong: Sulfur dioxide released, which then causes acid rain to form

items.q: The share of UK electricity generated from renewables has risen sharply. Why?
items.correct: Concern about climate change has driven investment in renewables
items.misconception: Renewable schemes have always been the cheapest option there is
items.why: The scientific case for reducing fossil fuel use is clear, so students assume that anything preventing change must be a failure to understand it. Set out the real obstacles: new schemes cost a great deal up front and take years to build, existing vehicles, boilers and power stations were designed for fossil fuels, jobs and industries depend on them, and some renewables are less reliable.
items.random_wrong: Fossil fuels ran out completely, so nothing else was left to use

items.q: Fossil fuels still supply much of the world's energy. Why is the change away so slow?
items.correct: Building new schemes costs a great deal and takes many years
items.misconception: Renewable resources have already replaced them almost everywhere
items.why: News coverage highlights records and milestones for renewable generation, and students generalise a growing share into a completed replacement. Read trends carefully: a rising share is not a finished change. Transport and heating in particular still run largely on oil and gas, and the change is limited by cost, existing equipment and reliability.
items.random_wrong: Scientists do not agree that fossil fuels harm the environment

items.q: Scientists identified the harm caused by burning fossil fuels, yet their use goes on. Why?
items.correct: Political, social, ethical and economic factors limit what is done
items.misconception: Science can always solve a problem once it has identified it
items.why: School science shows problems being solved, so students expect an answer to follow every problem. The distinction between knowing what is wrong and being able to act on it is not obvious. Identifying an issue and dealing with it are different things. What is actually done depends on political decisions, on what society will accept, on ethical judgements and on economic cost - and none of those is settled in a laboratory.
items.random_wrong: The evidence for the harm is not accepted by most scientists

items.q: Is bio-fuel non-renewable because burning it releases carbon dioxide?
items.correct: Bio-fuel is renewable, because the plants used to make it can be grown again as it is used.
items.misconception: Bio-fuel gets burned and gives off carbon dioxide just like coal, so it must be a non-renewable fuel too.
items.why: Students classify by what happens at the point of use - burning and smoke - rather than by whether the supply is replaced. Bio-fuel behaves like a fossil fuel in a burner, so it gets filed with them. Classify by replenishment. A crop grown this year and burned this year is replaced by next year's crop, so bio-fuel is renewable. Coal took millions of years to form and is not being replaced at the rate it is used.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are the tides unreliable because they depend on the weather?
items.correct: The tides follow a regular, predictable cycle that does not depend on the weather, so they are a reliable resource.
items.misconception: The tides are part of the sea, and the sea is controlled by the weather, so tidal energy is as unpredictable as wind or waves.
items.why: Tides, waves and wind all get grouped as 'natural, outdoor, weather things'. Students do not separate the daily tidal rhythm from the state of the sea surface. Separate tides from waves. Tide tables are printed years in advance because the cycle is predictable; wave height cannot be printed years ahead because it depends on the wind. Tides are reliable, waves are not.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does geothermal energy come from the Sun warming the ground?
items.correct: Geothermal energy comes from hot rock beneath the Earth's surface.
items.misconception: The ground is warm because the Sun has been shining on it, so geothermal energy is really just stored solar energy.
items.why: Students' direct experience of warm ground is a sunny day, and the everyday explanation for anything warm outdoors is the Sun. Geothermal schemes drill deep into rock that is hot day and night, in winter as well as summer, and in places where the surface is under snow. That is why geothermal is reliable and solar is not.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an electric car use no energy resource?
items.correct: An electric car uses whichever resources generated the electricity it was charged with.
items.misconception: Electric cars run on electricity rather than fuel, so they use no energy resource and cause no environmental impact.
items.why: There is no exhaust pipe and nothing is burned in the vehicle, so the environmental impact is invisible to the user. Students treat electricity as a resource in its own right. Electricity is not an energy resource: it has to be generated from one. If the electricity came from a coal station, carbon dioxide was released; if it came from wind, very little was. The impact moves, it does not disappear.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is carbon dioxide the gas that causes acid rain?
items.correct: Sulfur dioxide, released when fuels containing sulfur are burned, contributes to acid rain. Carbon dioxide contributes to global warming.
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is the pollutant from burning fuels, so it must be behind acid rain as well as everything else.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is the one gas from burning that students can name confidently, so it gets attached to every environmental problem they meet. Pair each gas with its own problem: carbon dioxide with global warming and climate change, sulfur dioxide with acid rain. Coal and oil contain sulfur impurities; that is where the sulfur dioxide comes from.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is nuclear fuel a type of fossil fuel because it is mined?
items.correct: Nuclear fuel is a separate resource from the fossil fuels. The fossil fuels are coal, oil and gas.
items.misconception: Uranium is dug out of the ground like coal, so nuclear fuel belongs with the fossil fuels.
items.why: Students use 'comes out of the ground' as the defining feature of a fossil fuel, instead of 'formed from the remains of organisms'. Both being non-renewable strengthens the link. Fossil fuels formed from the remains of living organisms and are burned. Uranium is a metal from rock and is not burned. They share only the label non-renewable.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are fossil fuels renewable because more is still forming underground?
items.correct: Fossil fuels are non-renewable, because they are not being replenished at anything like the rate at which they are used.
items.misconception: New coal and oil are still forming below the ground, so fossil fuels are being replenished and count as renewable.
items.why: The definition says 'being replenished', and it is true that the process has not stopped. Students apply the definition without weighing the rate against the rate of use. Compare the timescales. Fossil fuels take millions of years to form; the world burns them in decades. Replenishment that slow is no replenishment at all in practice, so they are non-renewable.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do solar resources supply nothing except on bright summer days?
items.correct: Solar output falls when it is cloudy, in winter and at night, but is not zero whenever the Sun is not shining brightly. The point is that output cannot be relied on.
items.misconception: Solar panels only work in strong sunshine, so in a cloudy country they simply do not work.
items.why: The reliability argument is remembered as a blunt 'solar does not work here', which is an overcorrection of a fair point about variable output. State the argument precisely: output varies with time of day, season and cloud, so the supply cannot be guaranteed when it is wanted. That is why solar is classed as unreliable, not because it produces nothing.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are bio-fuel and fossil fuel the same kind of resource?
items.correct: They are different resources. Bio-fuel is renewable; fossil fuels are non-renewable.
items.misconception: Both came from living things and both get burned, so bio-fuel and coal must belong to the same group.
items.why: The origin story of fossil fuels - formed from the remains of organisms - sounds like the origin of bio-fuel, and both are combusted. The difference is time and replacement. Bio-fuel comes from a crop grown this year that can be grown again; coal comes from organisms that lived millions of years ago and is not being replaced as it is used.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a resource unreliable if it damages the environment?
items.correct: Reliability and environmental impact are separate judgements. A resource can be reliable and damaging, or clean and unreliable.
items.misconception: Coal is bad for the environment, so it must be one of the unreliable resources; wind is clean, so it must be reliable.
items.why: Students sort resources onto a single good-bad scale, so every favourable word attaches to one group and every unfavourable word to the other. Judge each resource twice, on two separate questions. Coal is reliable but damaging. Wind is much cleaner but unreliable. Geothermal happens to be both reliable and clean - but that has to be shown, not assumed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does taking energy from the wind use the wind up?
items.correct: Wind is renewable: it is continually replenished, so using it does not exhaust the supply.
items.misconception: If turbines take energy out of the wind, then over time there will be less wind, so wind is being used up like a fuel.
items.why: Students apply the fuel model - a store that empties - to every resource, and the definition of renewable is not yet doing the work of distinguishing a store from a flow. Apply the definition: is it being replenished as it is used? Wind is continually replenished, so it is renewable. Compare with coal, which is a store built up over millions of years and not replaced as it is burned.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.1.3 National and global energy resources
